questions.stem: According to Mahābhārata 12.110.11, the word 'Dharma' is derived from which Sanskrit verbal root?
stem_variants: From which root does the term 'Dharma' originate as cited in Śānti Parva 12.110.11?
options: dhṛ (meaning to hold, bear, or uphold)
questions.answer: dhṛ (meaning to hold, bear, or uphold)
accepted_answers: dhṛ (meaning to hold, bear, or uphold)
questions.explanation: In Śānti Parva 12.110.11, Dharma is explicitly derived from the verbal root 'dhṛ' (dhāraṇe), signifying that which upholds, sustains, and holds society together.
questions.source_quote: Dharma is defined (12.110.11) as that which upholds the people, from the root dhṛ, 'to uphold'.

questions.stem: In Bhīṣma's administrative model for the kingdom, what is the precise ascending order of village groupings overseen by appointed heads?
stem_variants: Which sequence correctly outlines Bhīṣma's village administration tiers?
questions.explanation: Bhīṣma prescribes an administrative hierarchy consisting of a head for a single village, then tiers for 10, 20, 100, and 1,000 villages, each tier reporting upward.
questions.source_quote: Bhīṣma recommends a head for every village, one for ten villages, then twenty, hundred and thousand, each reporting upward...

questions.stem: In the Sabhā Parva, what protocol does Sage Nārada recommend to Yudhiṣṭhira regarding intelligence gathering on the 'tīrthas' (key state offices)?
stem_variants: How should intelligence operatives be organized and distributed across the tīrthas according to Nārada?
options: Deploy triads of mutually unacquainted spies to monitor 18 tīrthas of the adversary and 15 of one's own domain
Deploy pairs of related spies to monitor 15 tīrthas of the adversary and 18 of one's own domain
Assign four rotating spies to each of the 33 internal tīrthas without monitoring foreign courts
Use single undercover ascetics to inspect 12 ministerial tīrthas in both allied and enemy territories
distractor_pool: Deploy triads of spies to monitor all 33 tīrthas strictly within the capital
Appoint five overt ambassadors across 18 foreign ministries
questions.answer: Deploy triads of mutually unacquainted spies to monitor 18 tīrthas of the adversary and 15 of one's own domain
accepted_answers: Deploy triads of mutually unacquainted spies to monitor 18 tīrthas of the adversary and 15 of one's own domain
questions.explanation: Nārada asks Yudhiṣṭhira if he employs groups of three spies, unknown to one another, to inspect the eighteen tīrthas on the enemy's side and fifteen tīrthas within his own administration.
questions.source_quote: Nārada asks Yudhiṣṭhira whether he uses groups of three spies unknown to each other to learn about the eighteen tīrthas... on the other side and fifteen on his own.

questions.stem: How does Kṛṣṇa philosophically justify sanctioning the breaches of warfare conduct during the killings of Karṇa and Duryodhana?
stem_variants: What is the ethical rationale articulated by Kṛṣṇa when setting aside conventional rules of engagement against Karṇa and Duryodhana?
options: Unconventional or retaliatory tactics are justified as a last resort against adversaries who have systematically abandoned Dharma and weaponized its norms in bad faith
Kings and warriors are inherently exempt from karmic retributions during an officially declared Dharmayuddha
Adharma is an equally valid tactical path to victory whenever a righteous king faces military defeat
Warfare inherently operates beyond the realm of morality, rendering all ethical distinctions void on the battlefield
distractor_pool: Arjuna and Bhīma possessed absolute divine mandate to eliminate enemies by any arbitrary method
Balarāma’s strict adherence to rules was declared an invalid heresy by the assembled sages
questions.answer: Unconventional or retaliatory tactics are justified as a last resort against adversaries who have systematically abandoned Dharma and weaponized its norms in bad faith
accepted_answers: Unconventional or retaliatory tactics are justified as a last resort against adversaries who have systematically abandoned Dharma and weaponized its norms in bad faith
questions.explanation: The text explains that Kṛṣṇa does not advocate adharmic methods as a standard practice, but reserves them as a vital last resort against opponents who systematically embodied adharma and cynically invoked Dharma only when vulnerable.
questions.source_quote: The point: Kṛṣṇa does not advocate adharmic means in all battles but as a last resort against enemies who themselves used adharma.

questions.stem: In the Janaka-Brāhmaṇa dialogue recounted in the Anugītā (Aśvamedhika Parva), what essential realization proved King Janaka's qualification to turn the 'dharma-cakra' toward Brahma-prāpti?
stem_variants: Why did Dharmarāja, disguised as an exiled Brāhmaṇa, deem King Janaka worthy of turning the dharma-cakra in the Anugītā?
options: He recognized that the territory belonged neither to himself nor his ancestors, conquering his senses and renouncing 'mamatā' to rule purely for the welfare of others
He demonstrated complete legal jurisdiction over every parcel of land by citing ancestral Vedic grants
He abdicated his throne immediately and took up ascetic sannyāsa in the forest to eliminate royal guilt
He proved that a kṣatriya ruler possesses superior spiritual knowledge compared to an ordained brāhmaṇa
distractor_pool: He established a comprehensive taxation system that eliminated all poverty throughout Mithilā
He defeated Dharmarāja in a formal debate on ritual sacrifice and caste duties
questions.answer: He recognized that the territory belonged neither to himself nor his ancestors, conquering his senses and renouncing 'mamatā' to rule purely for the welfare of others
accepted_answers: He recognized that the territory belonged neither to himself nor his ancestors, conquering his senses and renouncing 'mamatā' to rule purely for the welfare of others
questions.explanation: Upon being asked where his kingdom begins and ends, Janaka introspected and realized the land did not belong to him or his ancestors; having conquered his senses and relinquished mamatā (possessiveness/mineness), he governed solely as an unattached instrument of Dharma, qualifying him for Brahma-prāpti.
questions.source_quote: Janaka reflected and realised the land belonged neither to him nor his forefathers; he had conquered his five senses and mind, given up mamatā and acted only for others' benefit. The Brāhmaṇa was Dharmarāja in disguise, who said such a king... is fit to turn the dharma-cakra... whose goal is Brahma-prāpti (MB 14.32.25).
